item.description:

item.title: What to expect as Hurricane Isaias bears down on the Gulf Coast as a major storm
item.description:
The hurricane approaching the northern Gulf Coast has been upgraded to a major Category 3 with maximum sustained winds of 120 mph — and it threatens to bring heavy rain, severe flooding, tornadoes, and power outages to the western Florida Panhandle, Alabama, Mississippi, and other parts of the Southeast. Hurricane Isaias, the first of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, is set to make landfall near the Pensacola, Florida, area Friday evening with a life-threatening storm surge of up to 9 feet. Coastal Alabama to Port St. Joe could also see 5 to 7 feet. Forecasters expect some weakening before the hurricane hits land, but warn Isaias will remain dangerous regardless of its exact strength. Mandatory evacuation orders have been issued for several coastal counties. item.title: India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest
item.description:

Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll. item.title: ‘Digger’ has a lot of haters. Here’s why they’re wrong.
item.description:
Last week, this magazine published a review of Digger , the new climate change allegory from Mexican provocateur Alejandro Iñárritu. In it, my colleague Jake Bittle explains in detail why he “ hated it .” I was skeptical of the bad reviews that Digger has been getting; after all, I like more of the Iñárritu films I’ve seen than not. I would even call one of them (his 2001 debut, Amores Perros ) a cinematic masterpiece. ( Birdman was fine.) In any case, most of the time a Mexican person is in the news, I am invested in their success, so I decided to see the movie for myself. Even then — two hours, nine minutes, and a small popcorn later — I was surprised by my reaction: I simply loved the movie. item.title: Unpacking the Environmental Issues in Susan Collins’ Tough Race in Maine
item.description:
BATH, Maine — Election after election, Republican Sen. Susan Collins has defied national political winds to return to office, representing a state that has backed Democrats in every presidential contest since 1992. But her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, is betting that her eight-year-old vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh and the Supreme Court’s subsequent overturning of federal abortion rights will persuade voters to sweep her out of office. item.title: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’
item.description:
Three years into Israel's genocide in Gaza, Palestinian human rights lawyer and legal scholar Noura Erakat argues that Donald Trump's Board of Peace is about more than Gaza: it's a blueprint for a new world order. Drop Site's Sharif Abdel Kouddous speaks with Erakat, a professor at Rutgers University, about her Boston Review essay, "Exit and Exception." Erakat argues that the Board of Peace matters less for whether it succeeds than for what it reveals: a political project, driven by market fundamentalists and a tech elite, to exit international law and popular democracy altogether. item.title: French cycling prodigy Seixas claims first Monument victory at Giro di Lombardia
item.description:
Cor Vos Nobody expects more from Paul Seixas than Paul Seixas. After a disappointing end to the World Championship road race where he cramped out of the lead group, the Frenchman's face was a picture, and his reflexive assessment biting. Less than two weeks later, the only-just-20-year-old turned up at his third-ever Monument and went solo 18 km from the line to become the youngest Il Lombardia winner in history. I don't really care about being the youngest or whatever, I just care about winning. Today I won a Monument and that's beautiful, that's all I will remember."
